what_it_does: Researchers have started using machine-learning models at runtime to predict program behavior — for example, predicting which code paths a program will take next, in order to strip out unused code paths (called code debloating) or enforce that only expected paths are allowed to execute (called control-flow integrity, a security mechanism). The problem is that ML models make occasional mispredictions even on benign inputs, which means a security monitor based on such a model might incorrectly block a normal program execution or, worse, fail to distinguish a misprediction from an actual attack. This paper takes a different approach: instead of trying to make the ML model more accurate everywhere, it uses static analysis — careful mathematical reasoning about the program done once before it ever runs — to enumerate all behaviors that are provably safe. Those provably-safe behaviors are removed from the ML model's decision space entirely. The ML model then only needs to classify a much smaller, genuinely ambiguous set of behaviors, where the chance of a misprediction being confused with a real attack is much lower.
